claims.text: As-received Q235 steel contains inherent microstructural defects and inclusions and represents a relatively defect-rich baseline.
Localized corrosion in untreated Q235 steel initiates preferentially at grain boundaries, inclusions, and surface heterogeneities.
Defect sites concentrate localized anodic activity.
Preferential oxidation of iron at defect sites produces porous, non-protective oxide or hydroxide layers.
A dense, stable passivating film can suppress corrosion in a NaCl environment.
Elevated temperature increases ionic mobility and anodic dissolution kinetics at active sites.
Faster dissolution at elevated temperature prevents stable passivation and accelerates pitting and generalized corrosion.
Mechanical polishing or thermal annealing can reduce or homogenize the relevant surface and near-surface defect population in Q235 steel.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl environment is applicable for evaluating corrosion behavior of a material system involving a Q235 steel substrate.
Defect-reduced Q235 samples should have a lower corrosion current density than untreated samples under identical exposure conditions.
Defect-reduced Q235 samples should develop fewer and smaller pits than untreated samples.
Defect-reduced Q235 samples should exhibit a more noble open-circuit potential than untreated samples.
The corrosion-resistance benefit of defect reduction should become more pronounced at elevated temperature.
The proposed defect-mediated mechanism applies at ambient and moderately elevated temperatures in chloride-rich environments.
The influence of defect-mediated corrosion may diminish when acids or sulfides dominate or when another mechanism produces complete passivation.
Residual stresses and minor alloying impurities may modify the corrosion behavior of Q235 steel.

The absence of significant electrochemical and pitting differences between treated and untreated samples under both temperature conditions would falsify defect density as the governing cause in the tested conditions.
